newsitem.title: UK: British financial watchdogs see staff turnover rise.
newsitem.headline: British financial watchdogs see staff turnover rise.

text.p: Staff are leaving key British financial watchdogs due to attractive offers from the firms they regulate and uncertainty over the post-election regulatory structure.
Insiders report a marked increase in staff turnover in recent months, but views differ on why people are leaving the "frontline" regulators.
"I think you'll find all regulators have noticed an increase in staff movement since December," one regulatory source told Reuters.
Some argue this is symptomatic of booming market conditions, particularly in investment banking and fund management where bonuses have rocketed.
Individuals versed in the intricacies of regulatory compliance are being offered packages which the regulators are struggling to match.
Questions over how a future Labour government might restructure the existing system and the fear of job cuts also appear to be taking their toll.

At present the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) oversees Self-Regulating Organisations (SROs) which authorise firms in investment business, monitor them, handle complaints and punish rule-breakers.

But the existing system, established by the Financial Services Act of 1986, would be altered by an incoming Labour government, if the opposition can wrest power from the ruling Conservatives in the May 1 general elections.
Labour believes the way City firms are regulated at present to be overly bureaucratic and expensive and would merge the overall manager of the system, the SIB, with the SROs.

While it has yet to spell out its plans in detail, regulators say the people whose jobs would be at risk would be at the top and bottom of the three SROs, the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA), the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) and the Personal Investment Authority (PIA). Regulatory sources say a merger of these under the SIB roof would lead to a combining of the financial operations of the three, as well as a paring down of support staff as the new body sought to achieve cost savings.
At present each has a chief executive, responsible for the day-to-day running of the organisation, and a part-time chairman. This leaves clear room for streamlining if all three were merged.
The SFA said there is no evidence that political uncertainty or staff concerns about their careers are leading to an increase in movement.

"There's no indication that the people who are leaving SFA are doing so because of uncertainty over their careers," its spokesman said. The SFA employs 270 people, of which 31 are operations personnel.
"Staff leaving here are basically going for commercial reasons," he said.

Compliance specialists, in demand following recent high-profile failings in several big firms, are in short supply. Many have cut their teeth as regulators, which the regulating authorities are seen as a fertile training ground for the banks and investment firms.

But for the SFA, competition with the industry is not a problem for recruitment. "Certainly in particular types of jobs in order to attract the right sort of person you have to offer the right sort of salary," the spokesman said.
But many SFA interviewees do ask about the effects any reform would have on the regulatory structure and how this might shape their careers.
The PIA said an atmosphere where regulators are sought after by the industry is a healthy one.
"PIA does not have a staff retention problem. We also encourage an interchange of staff between the industry and regulators as we consider that beneficial to both," its spokesman said.
The PIA, which employs more than 400 people, has a staff turnover of 14 percent a year.
